notes: Routing table, ARP cache and /etc/hosts reveal internal subnets and neighbouring hosts for pivoting; resolv.conf points at the internal DNS. Useful even when local privesc stalls - it feeds lateral movement. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 17 (Linux Privilege Escalation).

recommended.note: Sniff the wire if you can read traffic.

name: Enumeration - Network Information
description: Map the host's network position: interfaces, hosts file, routing, DNS, ARP neighbours, and who is/was logged in - useful for pivoting and finding other targets.

variations.label: Interfaces / hosts
variations.description: Shows network interface configuration including IP addresses, subnets, and additional network segments. Identifies dual-homed hosts for pivoting to other networks.

variations.label: Routing / DNS / ARP
variations.description: Lists active network connections and listening ports. Identifies internal services, database connections, and potential pivoting targets not visible from external scans.

variations.label: Logged-in users
variations.description: Shows the last login time for all user accounts. Identifies accounts that are actively used versus dormant accounts.

explain:
Maps the host's network position for pivoting and finding new targets:
  ip a                     list interfaces and their addresses
The variations cover /etc/hosts, routing (route/netstat -rn), DNS (resolv.conf), ARP neighbours (arp -a), and who is/was logged in (w/who/lastlog) - together they show what else is reachable from this box.
